blocks.x: Decision models wrapped in policy bounds, challenger benchmarks and explainable outputs: decisions a regulator can read, a panel can challenge, and a board can defend — with defer-to-human paths that are designed, not improvised.
A decision system is judged by its worst defensible case
blocks.sub: Design for the decision a regulator will read, not the average case

blocks.x: Decision intelligence is where analytics stops advising and starts acting: credit lines, fraud holds, service credits, triage priorities. That step from report to action is governed differently — the decision needs a policy envelope, a challenger, an explanation shape and an appeal path before it earns the right to act.

We build the envelope first: what the decision may consider, what it may not, what it must explain, when it must defer to a human, and how its quality is measured against a signed benchmark panel. Only then does the model inside get tuned.
Below: the failure modes that make decision models indefensible, the reference architecture that wraps them in challenge and explanation, and the console the risk committee reads.
The four defects that make a decision indefensible

The challenger scores every case, silently
blocks.sub: Champion-challenger economics and the disagreement triggers that keep autonomy honest

blocks.x: Every production decision is scored twice: the champion decides, the challenger disagrees silently. The disagreement rate is the most honest model-health metric available — it detects population drift months before accuracy metrics move, because challengers built on different features or different vintages fail in different places. Disagreement above threshold forces a review of the affected stratum before the next release, and the review is quantitative: which strata, which feature regime, which direction. This is the discipline that turns model risk management from an annual document into a weekly measurement.

The policy envelope is the second half of the defense. The champion only acts inside bounds signed by the risk owner — exposure ceilings, eligibility overlays, mandatory referral classes — and the explanation layer emits reason codes on every output, not on the samples an auditor requests. Reason-code coverage is therefore 100% by construction, and the appeal path routes to a named reviewer with the decision's full context, which is what a supervisory examination actually asks to see.

How do you keep model decisions explainable to regulators?
Every decision carries reason codes with 100% coverage, a feature-provenance trail and the challenger’s dissent where one exists. The explanation layer is part of the governed service, not a bolt-on.
What happens when the challenger and champion disagree?
Disagreement beyond signed tolerance routes the case to human review and triggers a calibration review. The disagreement ledger is itself a monitored asset — chronic dissent names the weaker model.
Can you work within our existing model-risk framework?

Yes. The gates map to model-risk examination expectations — inventory, validation, monitoring, controls — and the evidence pack is produced in your framework’s vocabulary, ready for the examination file.
How is fairness actually monitored, not just claimed?
Disparate-impact metrics run per protected class against signed tolerances. Drift beyond tolerance is a gate breach that blocks autonomy expansion — not a dashboard color.
Do you replace our models or wrap them?

We wrap first: policy envelope, challenger panel and explanation layer around your current model. Replacement happens only where the benchmark ledger shows a challenger earning it, quarter by quarter.
